summary: Source-level restructure: still one 256-thread workgroup per row, but each thread loads one contiguous 16-byte vector of x (global_load_dwordx4) instead of one float per loop iteration, keeps it in registers across the LDS reduction, and writes y from the registers, so x is read once instead of twice (a loop handles D > 1024, a scalar tail handles D % 4). 1.777x over amdclang at 240 pairs (CI 1.771 to 1.782), 65.2 us against a memory floor of 65.1 us: headroom 1.00. Case: the reference had headroom 1.8 because it re-read x and moved 4 bytes per lane per wait; the winner is now at the copy rate, so only fewer bytes could help further. Results meet the tolerance, not bit-identity (sum of squares is in another order).

friction: source() needs the full text resent for each define sweep even when only `defines` and `launch` change; a `source_like(state, defines, launch)` that reuses the stored text would make sweeps cheap.

Block size is in two places (the -D macro and launch.block) with nothing tying them: a mismatch would be silently wrong for the LDS array size. Letting launch expressions reference defines (or the reverse) would remove the trap.

No machine-level work was attempted after reaching headroom 1.00 (DPP reduction instead of the LDS tree, weight load issued before the barrier): no tool tells how much of the 65 us is the reduction; a probe with the reduction removed would have needed a hand-edited source.
lessons: Row-norm kernels from MIOpen (one workgroup per row, each thread looping over the row one float at a time, two passes over x): one 16-byte vector per thread held in registers across the reduction, so that x is read once, gave 1.78x and lands exactly on the copy floor (headroom 1.81 -> 1.00) at R=32768, D=1024. Use ext_vector_type(4) with aligned(4) to get global_load_dwordx4 / store_dwordx4 from amdclang.

Geometry at D=1024 (256 16-byte chunks per row): block 256 x 1 chunk per thread 1.777x; block 128 x 2 chunks 1.725x; block 64 x 4 chunks (one wave, no barriers at all) 1.571x. Spreading a row over 4 waves with 16 bytes per lane beats one wave with 64 bytes per lane even though it costs barriers, consistent with the copy-kernel finding that 64 bytes per lane is 0.79.

Barriers are not the cost once the kernel is memory-bound: 9 barriers -> 1 (per-wave barrier-free LDS tree, then one barrier and a sum of 4 partials) measured parity (0.992, CI 0.987-0.995 by compare at 240 pairs).
coarsen factor 2 on the restructured LDS/barrier row kernel: 6% loss (1.774 -> 1.658), same direction as on the reference (0.97 to 1.00).

A barrier-free LDS tree inside one wave (lid & 63 indexing, threads 64w..64w+63 in lockstep) compiled by amdclang from plain __shared__ code passes the full battery, including at block 256 with one barrier before the cross-wave read.

session.final:
`mo_t5_layernorm` is now **1.78x** faster than amdclang's build (state `ea52679a9f99e567`, 240 pairs, CI 1.771–1.782), verified by static check and the full 77-case battery. The report is recorded.

- **What changed:** still one 256-thread workgroup per row, but each thread loads one contiguous 16-byte vector of `x`, keeps it in registers across the reduction, and writes `y` from those registers. `x` is read once instead of twice. A loop covers `D > 1024` and a scalar tail covers `D % 4`.
- **Which case this is:** the reference had headroom 1.8 because it re-read `x` and moved 4 bytes per lane per wait. The winner runs at 65.2 us against a memory floor of 65.1 us (headroom 1.00), so only moving fewer bytes could help further.
- **Accuracy:** results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical, because the sum of squares is accumulated in a different order.

| Variant | State | Speedup vs amdclang |
|---|---|---|
| Block 256, one chunk per thread, original 9-barrier tree (shipped) | `ea52679a9f99e567` | 1.777 |
| Same, with one barrier instead of nine | `34f0ace93da02efd` | 1.774 (parity with shipped) |
| Block 128, two chunks per thread | `d09cb4b4095efd8f` | 1.725 |
| `coarsen` factor 2 on the one-barrier variant | `b636a82599eab92c` | 1.658 |
| Block 64, one wave per row, no barriers | `ecfe5f1caf42d3e8` | 1.571 |

I stopped after seven timings because the last three ideas of different kinds (flatter reduction, another block size, `coarsen`) each brought nothing over the best state. No machine-IR edits were tried beyond `coarsen`; a DPP reduction or an earlier weight load remain untested.
